units.title: What Kind of Book Is This?
units.sub: A pharmacy bag says “three times a day.” A love letter says “three times a day” too. Misread the genre, and however sincere you are, you will misread the meaning.

share.v: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,

blocks.h: When John wrote his Gospel, he had no idea he was writing “John 3:16.” Today’s chapter divisions can be traced to a system from around 1205 by Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury. The New Testament’s verses were not numbered until 1551, by Robert Estienne, a printer from Paris.

Even its house numbers were nailed on later, yet by early 2026 this ancient book existed in complete form in 795 languages, and at least portions of it existed in 4,121. Of the world’s roughly 7,393 languages, 3,272 still do not have a single verse.
Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
A library you can carry

The English word “Bible” comes from the Greek ta biblia, literally the plural “books.” The Protestant Bible has 39 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New, 66 in all. The Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments have more books, which the next gallery, “The Canon,” will discuss.

There are three languages. The Old Testament is mainly Hebrew, while Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12-26, Daniel 2:4–7:28 and Jeremiah 10:11 are in Aramaic. The New Testament is in the Greek commonly spoken at the time.
Genre is the first key to reading

A pharmacy bag says, “Three times a day, after meals.” A love letter says, “I think of you three times a day.” Both say “three times.” The first one you must follow by the number; if you start counting on the second, the person who wrote it will probably get upset. The Bible holds genealogies, law codes, love poems, laments, visions and personal letters, and each has its own way of being read.

items: Narrative (Genesis, Acts): records what happened, and recording something does not mean approving of it. Watch how the whole book evaluates it.
Law (Exodus, Leviticus): the terms of God’s covenant with ancient Israel. Ask how it is fulfilled in Christ.
Poetry (Psalms, Song of Solomon): speaks in images. “Yahweh is my rock” is no geological report.

Wisdom (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes): mostly gives general patterns, not guarantees. In Proverbs 26:4-5, two verses side by side, one says not to answer a fool according to his folly and the other says to answer him, which is exactly how the reader learns to discern the moment.
Prophets: spoke first to the people of their own day, with judgment and with hope, and in part they point to the future.
Gospels and letters: the former are ancient biographies centered on Jesus. With the latter, first ask who they were written to and what the occasion was.
Apocalyptic (the second half of Daniel, Revelation): full of symbols. Use it to build a timetable from the newspaper headlines, and you will most likely get it wrong.

blocks.h: Reading by genre does not mean pushing every difficulty off onto metaphor. Genre helps us hear the author; it is no way around sentences we dislike. For how to read this book, the introduction by Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart is an excellent place to start.

The Bible’s narrative can be seen like this: creation, fall, the choosing of Israel, the coming of Christ, the sending of the church, and the renewal of all things. Bartholomew and Goheen explain this main storyline as a “drama in six acts.”
Is “about 40 authors over about 1,500 years” reliable?

This is an estimate commonly used in church circles, and we must be honest about its conditions. It places the Pentateuch in the time of Moses, and it counts the traditional authors of many books. Many psalms have no known author, the Gospels are not signed in their text, and to this day no one knows who wrote Hebrews. So the figure is best treated as a rough range and not as a statistic.

items.h: Largely affirms the traditional authors of the books while also accepting editing and the use of secretaries. Carson and Moo discuss the books one by one and defend Paul’s authorship of the Pauline letters.

Largely holds that the Pentateuch took shape over a long period, in part around the time of the exile. Many also regard some Pauline letters and 2 Peter as pseudonymous. John J. Collins’s introduction can represent this reading.

Evangelicals themselves differ on how to define the Bible’s authority. The 2013 volume Five Views on Biblical Inerrancy sets several evangelical scholars’ positions side by side, and the 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy is an important point of reference among them.

blocks.h: The skeptic’s strongest question is this: could this main storyline have been created by later editors and by the church, as they selected and ordered the books? Indeed, the arrangement of the canon is itself a kind of reading. Consistency can have a human element, so it cannot by itself prove that the Bible comes from God. What we can say is that this consistency deserves an explanation, and the Christian explanation is that He revealed Himself step by step in history.

Ancient Israel and the Mediterranean world were largely oral societies, where much content first circulated through telling and memorizing and was written down later. Walton and Sandy argue that reading the Old Testament with today’s picture of “an author finishing a book in his own hand” easily leads to asking the wrong questions. They remain evangelical scholars who believe in the Bible’s authority.

The Chinese Union Version in the hands of Chinese readers has its own story. An interdenominational team of missionaries began translating in 1890, publishing the New Testament in 1906 and the whole Bible in 1919. Its influence has been enormous, yet it is a translation, with its own mistranslations and outdated terms, which is why revisions came later.
Let’s look separately at the numbers, the ways of reading, and the inferences.
The Bible is composed of works from different eras, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. The Protestant edition has 66 books; other traditions have different numbers.

As of January 1, 2026, United Bible Societies counted the complete Bible in 795 languages, the New Testament in 1,815, and portions only in 1,511. Since 1946 a cumulative total of more than 25 billion Bibles or parts of Bibles (including single books and selections) have been distributed.
Chapter and verse divisions were added later. Chapters began around the early 13th century, and New Testament verse numbering began in 1551.

“About 40 authors over about 1,500 years” is a common estimate, on condition that one accepts most of the traditional authors and dates. Scholars who do not accept them arrive at a shorter span of time and a different number of authors.
The authorship and date of individual books are still debated among scholars, and evangelical and critical scholars often reach different conclusions.

These very different books together point to one Christ, which Christians see as the one God revealing Himself step by step in history. This is an interpretation of faith, and statistics cannot prove it.
He spoke at many times and in various ways

God could simply have dropped an instruction manual from heaven. Instead He chose to speak through shepherds, kings, exiles, fishermen and tax collectors, in their languages and their genres. This is a God willing to stoop down to us.
God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son,
Every shelf in the library finally points to the same Person. The risen Jesus walked along the road to Emmaus, two disheartened disciples did not recognize Him, and He started explaining from Moses.
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

To the people who knew the Bible best, Jesus also said something every Bible reader should remember: you can know the book thoroughly and still miss its main character. The Bible’s goal is to bring us before the Lord who died for us and rose from the dead.
“You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me.

Open your Bible’s table of contents and slowly run your eyes over the book titles, noticing the poems, law codes, letters and visions among them. Consider this: God used all these ways just so that you could know Him.
Reflect: Do I usually read every passage in the same way? Do I read the Bible to get answers, or to meet Jesus?

Prayer: Lord, you have spoken to people at many times and in various ways, and finally you have shown yourself to us through your Son. May the Holy Spirit open my heart, so that I read your word rightly and meet, in its words, the Christ who laid down His life for me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: a standard must be understood before it can be used. I will not treat poetry as statute, or use a single verse to back up what I have already decided.
Jesus is my example: this is how He Himself read Scripture, explaining from Moses to Himself. With every book, ask: how does this point to Christ?
Change your mindset → change your life → change your living: first change the mindset that “the Bible is a reference book for looking up answers,” and your attitude toward reading it will change.

blocks.h: This week: choose a short book you have never read (Ruth or Philippians, for example) and read it in one sitting. Before you start, look up its genre and who it was written to. Then write one sentence about it to a brother or sister.
Pass it on: Which part of the Bible have you read? If it were a library, which kind of book would you most want to pull out first?
Quiz

quiz.q: Roughly when were the New Testament “verses” we use today numbered?
o: In the 1st century AD, by the apostles themselves
In Estienne’s Greek New Testament of AD 1551
When the Chinese Union Version was published in 1919
quiz.e: Estienne numbered the verses in 1551. The original authors wrote without any chapter or verse numbers.

quiz.q: About “about 40 authors over about 1,500 years,” which statement is most accurate?
o: It is a common estimate that depends on accepting the traditional authors and dates
It is a statistic all scholars agree on
The biblical books themselves state these two numbers
quiz.e: This estimate has conditions, and stating them is what makes the citation honest.

quiz.q: Proverbs 26:4-5, two adjacent verses, give opposite answers. What is the most reasonable reading?
o: It proves Proverbs got it wrong
Only one of the two verses is true Scripture
The wisdom genre wants us to discern the moment according to the situation
quiz.e: Proverbs mostly gives general patterns, and the two verses are set side by side so that we will discern the situation.

units.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
units.sub: Dig up a thousand-year-old notebook: the main ingredients have barely changed, and there are a few pinches of spice nobody else wrote down.

share.v: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.

blocks.h: “The word of our God stands forever.” You can read this famous line in the Great Isaiah Scroll, written more than two thousand years ago. Yet right before this sentence there is a stretch of text that another scribe added later.

The scribes turned to dust long ago, but the marks of their hands remain. This parchment scroll is about 7.3 meters long, with 54 columns, and it preserves all 66 chapters of Isaiah in the same order.
The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.
Seventy years ago, a leap of a thousand years

Between late 1946 and early 1947, Bedouin shepherds found the first scrolls in a cave near Qumran on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea. By 1956, 11 scroll caves had been discovered. The total varies with how they are classified; common counts run from a little over 900 to 981 manuscripts, drawn from tens of thousands of fragments. About 235 of them are biblical books. They date from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD.

Before this, the most complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts mostly came from around the 10th century AD. The Dead Sea Scrolls suddenly pushed the evidence back by about a thousand years, and for the first time they let scholars check what had happened during that thousand years.

Suppose your family has a recipe for braised pork handed down for more than ten generations. You might well suspect that the flavor drifted long ago. Then one day you dig a thousand-year-old notebook out of the wall of the old house. The main ingredients and proportions are roughly the same, and you breathe a sigh of relief. But a few pages add an extra pinch of star anise in a different hand, and another nephew’s version leaves one ingredient out. That is how the Dead Sea Scrolls felt to scholars: stable, and livelier than anyone imagined.
The Great Isaiah Scroll: what matches and what differs

The handwriting of the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) dates to about 125 to 100 BC, and the calibrated radiocarbon range is 356 to 103 BC. Compared with the later Masoretic Text, it has more than 2,600 variants. Most are small differences of spelling, single words and word order, and a few affect a whole verse. Another Isaiah scroll, 1QIsab, is quite close to the Masoretic Text.

You will often see claims online that the Great Isaiah Scroll is “95% word-for-word identical to today’s Bible.” That makes a complicated situation sound too simple. The more honest way to say it: the overall content and order are highly consistent, and the differences are real too.
The honest part: some differences are not small

items: The height of Goliath: the Chinese Union Version follows the Masoretic Text with “six cubits and a span” (1 Samuel 17:4), about 2.9 meters. 4QSama, the Septuagint and Josephus all have four cubits and a span, about 2 meters.

The brutality of Nahash: at the end of 1 Samuel 10, 4QSama has an extra passage explaining how Nahash, king of the Ammonites, gouged out the right eyes of the Gadites and Reubenites. Other Hebrew manuscripts lack it, and some modern translations (such as the NRSV) have adopted it.

Two versions of Jeremiah: the Septuagint is much shorter than the Masoretic Text and differs in order. At Qumran, 4QJerb is close to the Septuagint, while 4QJera is close to the Masoretic Text, which shows that the two forms once existed side by side.

Psalm 145: this is an acrostic poem, and the Masoretic Text is missing the verse that begins with the letter N. 11QPsa and the Septuagint have that verse, though some scholars think it was added later.

Deuteronomy 32:8: the Chinese Union Version follows the Masoretic Text with “the number of the children of Israel.” 4QDeutj has a reading along the lines of “sons of God,” the Septuagint is close to it, and many modern translations have adopted it.

blocks.h: These differences raise a genuine difficulty: should we speak of “the original text of the Bible,” or of several versions existing side by side?

items.h: Many scholars point out that the line of transmission that became the Masoretic Text was already very careful in the Second Temple period. Individual readings can be corrected from the scrolls, and the main body is reliable.

Eugene Ulrich and some other scholars argue that several literary versions of the scriptural books existed side by side at the time, and that what we now call the standard text took its fixed shape only later. Emanuel Tov has described the diversity of the text in detail.
Since versions can change, the claim that “not one word of God’s word has been altered” cannot stand. This criticism does land against the “never changed a word” way of speaking.

Traditionally evangelicals distinguish the inspiration of the original manuscripts from the transmission of the copies. Differences among copies can be studied and corrected, and the core message does not change because of them. How best to describe the “original manuscripts” is still being discussed among evangelicals themselves.

blocks.h: Who wrote them? Still no final answer

items.h: The long-standing mainstream view: Qumran was a base of the Essenes or a related sect, based on evidence that includes the description by the ancient writer Pliny the Elder and the Community Rule. Jodi Magness supports this from an archaeological angle.
Drawing on 4QMMT and other documents, Lawrence Schiffman argues that this group was connected with the Zadokite priestly tradition.
Norman Golb argues that the scrolls came from a number of libraries in Jerusalem and were hidden in the caves to escape the Roman army.
Yizhar Hirschfeld and others think Qumran was originally a Hasmonean-period fortress or a site with some other purpose, and may have had no direct connection with the scrolls.

blocks.h: Two more recent cautions. In 2025, Mladen Popović’s team published an AI handwriting-dating model called Enoch in PLOS One. Combining it with 24 new radiocarbon samples, they proposed that some scrolls may be older than previously estimated, with the Daniel fragment 4Q114 falling around 230 to 160 BC. Christopher Rollston and others do not consider this a revolutionary breakthrough and have criticized the reporting as overblown.

Also, in 2020 an independent report of more than 200 pages found that all 16 “Dead Sea Scroll” fragments held by the Museum of the Bible in the United States are modern forgeries: someone painted text onto old leather and then added a coating to make it look ancient. These were never scrolls formally excavated at Qumran, and the report did not shake the holdings of the Israel Museum. What believers should remember is this: a heart hungry for proof is exactly the forger’s market.
Here we mark separately what is certain, what is still being discussed and what is inference.

About 235 of the Dead Sea Scrolls are biblical books, roughly a thousand years older than the main manuscripts of the Masoretic Text. Every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther has been found, though some only in small fragments.
1QIsaa preserves all 66 chapters of Isaiah in the same order as the Masoretic Text, with more than 2,600 variants, most of them small.
The Old Testament manuscripts from Qumran are not all alike. The differences in books such as Samuel and Jeremiah are considerable, and some texts are closer to the Septuagint.

The repeated wording in Isaiah 40:7-8 was added to 1QIsaa as a later correction. De Troyer and Herbison argue that this is the longer form of the Masoretic tradition, and not something the Septuagint dropped.
As for who produced the scrolls, the Essene hypothesis still has wide support and has also been challenged from many sides. The results of AI handwriting dating are also still under discussion.

More than a thousand years of copying were broadly stable and also left differences that can be studied. In this Christians see the faithfulness of God, and they see Him using limited human beings. This is an interpretation of faith, which the scrolls themselves cannot prove.
People are grass, the word endures

The theme of Isaiah 40 is how fragile human beings are and how lasting God’s word is. Read at the mouth of a Qumran cave, it hits especially hard: the scribes passed away, the Roman army came, the temple burned, and those skin scrolls waited in the dark for nearly two thousand years.

For, “All flesh is like grass, and all of man’s glory like the flower in the grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the Lord’s word endures forever.” This is the word of Good News which was preached to you.

Peter says that the word that endures is the gospel. In a first-century synagogue in Nazareth, someone handed a scroll of Isaiah to a carpenter. That scroll and the Isaiah found by the Dead Sea belong to the same world of copying.

The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He opened the book, and found the place where it was written, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed,

The Great Isaiah Scroll also contains the poem of the Suffering Servant. It existed more than a century before Jesus was born, so this passage is no after-the-fact composition by the church. Jewish tradition and Christians differ on how to interpret this prophecy, and the next gallery in this hall will take that up. Christians believe that this Servant’s road ends at Calvary.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
Choose a passage you often read and copy it out by hand, slowly, stroke by stroke. Imagine a scribe in a room with no electric light, writing the very same sentence.
Reflect: What in my life do I assume is solid but is really like grass? What words am I willing to spend a lifetime passing on?

Prayer: Living God, people are like grass, yet Your word stands forever. Thank You for using so many nameless hands to bring Your word into mine. Help me to treasure this book and to rest secure in Christ, unafraid to face hard questions honestly. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: a standard deserves serious study. Looking into the differences is not irreverent; the scribes themselves checked their work this way.
Selflessness: the scribes of the scrolls left almost no names behind. I too can serve quietly and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Move from a temporary perspective to an eternal one: empires and temples will pass away, and God’s word will not. Set today’s gains and losses against that length of time.

blocks.h: This week: visit the Israel Antiquities Authority’s Leon Levy digital library or the Israel Museum’s Dead Sea Scrolls website, see the Great Isaiah Scroll with your own eyes, and read Isaiah 53 alongside it. Then copy out Isaiah 40:8 by hand and give it to someone going through a hard time.
Pass it on: if someone had copied a book for over a thousand years, leaving parts that are very stable along with some differences, would you trust it more, or doubt it more?
Quiz

quiz.q: What is the most honest way to describe the relationship between the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) and the Masoretic Text?
o: Identical down to the last word
The overall content and order are highly consistent, with over two thousand variants, most of them small
It is practically a different book
quiz.e: Both the consistency and the differences are facts. Don’t tell only half the story.

quiz.q: What do 4QSama and the Septuagint give as the height of Goliath?
o: Four cubits and a span
Six cubits and a span
Ten cubits
quiz.e: The Masoretic Text has six cubits; 4QSama, the Septuagint and Josephus have four.

quiz.q: What is the current situation regarding who wrote the scrolls?
o: It is settled that they were all written by Essenes
It is settled that they all came from the Jerusalem temple
The Essene hypothesis still has wide support and has also been challenged; there is no final answer yet
quiz.e: This question is still being researched, and in verification it should be marked as disputed.

units.title: New Testament Manuscripts
units.sub: There are more variants than there are words in the New Testament. That sentence is true; it just isn’t the whole story.

share.v: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

blocks.h: In a library in Manchester, England, there is a scrap of papyrus about the size of a credit card, roughly 8.9 × 6 centimeters, with Greek writing on both sides. It is often regarded as one of the oldest surviving manuscripts of the New Testament.
On a piece this small, very few words could survive. And yet the lines on the back copy what was said when the Roman governor questioned Jesus:
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?”
First, let’s be honest with the numbers

You often see “over 5,800 Greek New Testament manuscripts” online. In 2023, two scholars at the Institute for New Testament Textual Research (INTF) in Münster, Germany, recounted the official catalog and arrived at about 5,700 entries; after subtracting those that have been destroyed or whose whereabouts are unknown, about 5,541. Most of these are fragments or partial books, and complete New Testaments are a small minority. The figure will also keep shifting with new discoveries and the identification of duplicates.
The three earliest names

P52: a fragment of John 18, bought in Egypt in 1920 and published in 1935. The common date is around AD 125, but this rests only on a comparison of handwriting. Brent Nongbri, writing in both 2005 and 2020, pointed out that handwriting cannot be pinned down that precisely and that a reasonable range extends into the later second century or even the third. Orsini and Clarysse, for their part, proposed 125–175.

P46: a codex of Paul’s letters from about AD 200, originally about 104 leaves, of which 86 survive, held between the University of Michigan in the United States and the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin. Hebrews follows immediately after Romans.

Codex Sinaiticus: a fourth-century parchment codex containing the complete New Testament, with the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas added. Constantin von Tischendorf obtained it at St Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai, and in 1859 he saw the remaining pages. Whether he was right to take it away is still disputed; most of the pages are now in the British Library.

Suppose you give an important document to a thousand people to copy by hand, and then their students go on copying it. There will certainly be more typos, because there are more copyists. But to recover the original you also have a thousand copies that can be compared with one another. Where one person slipped, the others’ copies will show it. The work of New Testament textual research is, broadly, this kind of comparison.
That frightening number

In his bestseller Misquoting Jesus (2005), Bart Ehrman estimated 200,000 to 400,000 variants, more than the roughly 138,000 words of the Greek New Testament. That is true, and it may even be an undercount: Peter Gurry’s 2016 study estimated about 500,000 even without counting spelling. He also explained that this number mainly reflects how many times the text was copied, not any unfaithfulness on the part of the copyists.

Beyond the quantity, we need to look at the nature of the variants. Daniel Wallace sorts them into four categories, asking whether a difference changes the meaning and whether it could be the original reading. He estimates that those that both affect the meaning and have a chance of being original make up only about 1%. An example is 1 John 1:4: is it “our joy” or “your joy”?
Three passages we won’t hide

Mark 16:9-20 is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. John 7:53–8:11 (the woman caught in adultery) is absent from early witnesses such as P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and begins to appear in Greek manuscripts only around the fifth century. Most scholars think neither passage was part of the original work; many also think the John passage may preserve a genuine event from the life of Jesus. Modern Bible editions usually add a note.

Ehrman also cites harder examples. In Mark 1:41 a few manuscripts say Jesus was “angry,” while most say He was “moved with compassion”; even Wallace leans toward thinking “angry” may be the original, but Mark 3:5 already records Jesus’ anger, so the portrait is not overturned. In Hebrews 2:9 a few late manuscripts read “apart from God,” while most read “by the grace of God,” and the two scholars judge this differently.
Let’s take the claims one at a time and mark how certain each is.
There are about 5,700 Greek New Testament manuscripts (2023 count), mostly fragments; the number of variants runs into the hundreds of thousands.

P52 is one of the earliest New Testament manuscripts. Its date is judged by handwriting alone; the common range is around the second century, with the upper and lower limits still disputed, so we should no longer say it is “definitely AD 125.”
Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53–8:11 are absent from some of the earliest important manuscripts.

The “first-century Mark fragment” that circulated for years was dated, when formally published in 2018, to the late second or early third century. That publicity was wrong, and the Christian scholar involved publicly apologized.

The New Testament has far more Greek manuscripts than any other work of ancient Greek literature. The Iliad, with about 1,757, is the closest rival; counting methods differ, and the gap is smaller than older apologetics books claimed.

Having many manuscripts only helps us reconstruct what the authors wrote; whether what they wrote is true, the manuscripts cannot answer. Christians believe God’s word has been kept through the generations. That is a judgment of faith: textual research supports its reasonableness but cannot prove it for us.
Perspectives Room
How much do these variants matter for faith?

items.h: We do not have the originals, the manuscripts we have came later, and for the first few decades we can mostly see nothing of the copying. Some variants do change the meaning of a passage, even the reading of a whole book, and should not be passed over lightly. He also admits that the vast majority of variants are insignificant, and in an interview in the paperback edition he said his position does not conflict with the view of his teacher Metzger that the essential beliefs of Christianity are not affected by the variants.

The sheer numbers Ehrman stresses give an impression more drastic than Ehrman’s own actual position. He grants that the few passages Ehrman cites are indeed not original or are disputed, but maintains that to date no variant overturns a core doctrine of the New Testament.

The earliest manuscripts are rare, so the copying situation before the second century can only be inferred, and scholars still differ on which reading is original in a small number of passages. Both scholars acknowledge this.

blocks.h: God placed His words in the hands of people who make mistakes

The New Testament did not come down as a golden edition written by angels. What we hold are papyri from Egyptian rubbish heaps, parchment copied by monks until their hands ached, and slips of the pen, marginal notes and arguments. This is how God entrusted His word: through people, and finite people at that.
in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained.

This way fits how God saves people. He did not shout from across the sky. He entered history Himself and became someone who could be questioned and crucified. On that fragment, Pilate is asking “What is truth?” while the truth stands in front of him.

Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
So the end point of manuscript study is a person. John’s purpose in writing is direct: these things are recorded so that people will trust the risen Christ.
but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

Open your Bible and find a footnote in small print, for example “some ancient manuscripts read…”. Don’t skip it. Think about how many nameless copyists and how many scholars’ collations stand behind that line of small print so that this passage could reach your hands.
Meditate: Do I want a faith so flawless that it never has to face questions, or am I willing to let Jesus Himself answer my real questions?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the truth. Thank You for passing Your word down through so many nameless hands, generation after generation, until it reached mine. Save me from exaggerated testimony, and save me also from the pride of suspicion; let me hear Your voice and follow You, because You died and rose for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: a standard deserves to be taken seriously. When you meet a small-print footnote, look it up; don’t skip it, and don’t be afraid of it.
Humility overcomes pride: even a Christian scholar who over-promoted a find publicly apologized. I too can admit I was wrong, because glory does not depend on my saving face.
Change your mindset → change your life: move from “I want to win this debate” to “I want Jesus to be seen clearly.”

blocks.h: This week: read Mark 16 once, notice how verse 8 connects to verse 9, and then see how your Bible marks it. Tell a friend what you found.
Pass it on: Have you ever heard that “the Bible was changed many times”? How do you think one could check to see how far that statement is right?
Quiz

quiz.q: Which statement about the date of P52 is most accurate?
o: Radiocarbon dating has fixed it at AD 125
It is judged by handwriting; the common claim is about AD 125, and the range is still disputed
It is definitely a first-century manuscript
quiz.e: The date of P52 rests only on a comparison of ancient scripts, and scholars differ on the range.

quiz.q: The number of variants is very large. What does it mainly reflect?
o: The very large number of manuscripts and acts of copying
Copyists deliberately forging the text
That the original manuscript still exists
quiz.e: Gurry points out that this number mainly reflects how often the text was copied.

quiz.q: What does having many manuscripts help us do?
o: Prove that every sentence of the New Testament is true
Prove that Jesus rose from the dead
Reconstruct, with more confidence, what the authors originally wrote
quiz.e: The textual question and the question of historical truth are two different questions.

units.title: How Was the Canon Formed?
units.sub: The fake books fell off the altar by themselves? It makes a great story. The real process was slower, and it holds up better under checking.

share.v: knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.

blocks.h: AD 325, the Council of Nicaea. The bishops piled all the books on the altar, they prayed, and the false books fell to the floor while the true ones stayed on top.

This story first appears in a Greek document from about the ninth century, more than five hundred years after the council. In 1764 Voltaire used it to make a joke, and that is how it spread. The version many people believe today is that the emperor picked the Bible at Nicaea. Neither the surviving records of the council nor the eyewitnesses of the time mention any such thing.
knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.
What is the “canon”?

Canon originally meant a measuring rod, and later by extension a standard. The question of the New Testament canon is: which books count as the church’s authoritative Scriptures? This was not settled in a day. It took several hundred years, and the core stabilized early, with the arguments mainly at the edges.

A pharmacopoeia lists which medicines work, but a medicine does not work because it was written into the pharmacopoeia. The pharmacopoeia records facts that people recognized after using the medicines for generations. Christians view the canon in much the same way: the church was recognizing these books, not handing out authority to them. Critics will ask in return: who compiled this pharmacopoeia? Did the compilers have an agenda? That question will be handled honestly below.
A timeline

items: About AD 140: Marcion accepted only ten letters of Paul and one gospel similar to Luke, and rejected the Old Testament. The church rejected him, and this also forced everyone to answer the question: which books count?

About 180: Irenaeus argued that there are exactly four Gospels, no more and no fewer, and used the four quarters of the world and the four winds as an illustration. The illustration may be a stretch, but it shows that the four Gospels were already the mainstream by then.

The Muratorian Fragment: lists about 22 of the 27 books, and also mentions the Wisdom of Solomon and the Apocalypse of Peter; it recommends reading the Shepherd of Hermas but says it was written too recently to be read out in church as Scripture. Most scholars date it to the late second century, though some argue for the fourth.
About 330: Eusebius sorted books into three groups: recognized, disputed and rejected. James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2 and 3 John were among the disputed.
367: Athanasius’s thirty-ninth festal letter is the earliest surviving list that matches today’s 27 books exactly.
393 and 397: the regional councils of Hippo and Carthage listed the same books.

blocks.h: In making their judgments, the early church often asked three things: does it come from an apostle or someone connected with the apostles (apostolicity); is it widely used by churches in different places (catholicity); and does it agree with the gospel that was handed down (orthodoxy)?
What about the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of Judas?

The Gospel of Thomas has 114 sayings; the complete Coptic text came to light in 1945 at Nag Hammadi in Egypt, and Greek fragments had been found earlier at Oxyrhynchus. Scholars have no consensus on when it was written, and whether it is independent of the four Gospels is still disputed. The manuscript of the Gospel of Judas has been radiocarbon dated to about AD 220–340, and Irenaeus mentioned a work of that name around AD 180; scholars think it was composed in the second century. Amy-Jill Levine, one of the scholars involved in studying it, said it provides no new historical information about Jesus or Judas.
The Old Testament: a different story

At the end of the first century AD, Josephus said that the Jewish sacred books number 22. The old view that “the Council of Jamnia decided the Hebrew canon” has been questioned since 1964 by Jack Lewis and others, and is no longer accepted by most scholars today; when the canon took its final shape is still under discussion.

The Greek manuscripts used by early Christians often contained books beyond the Hebrew Bible, such as Tobit, Judith and the Maccabees, and the lists of books in different manuscripts were not consistent. Jerome favored the Hebrew original; Luther set these books apart in a separate section; the Catholic Church confirmed them as canonical at the Council of Trent in 1546; and the Orthodox Old Testament lists more still. The Protestant 39 books have the same content as the Hebrew Bible, only divided differently.

items.h: The Old Testament follows the Hebrew Bible; the Apocrypha may be read and are useful, but are not used as a basis for doctrine.
The second canon (the Deuterocanon) belongs to the Bible, based on long liturgical use and the church’s determination.

It rests on the Greek Old Testament tradition, with a few more books than the Catholic list. The traditions differ respectfully on the authority of these few books, and all three recognize the 27 books of the New Testament.

blocks.h: Let’s take the claims one at a time and mark how certain each is.

The Council of Nicaea (325) did not decide the list of biblical books. Neither the surviving records nor the eyewitnesses mention it; even Ehrman, a scholar who does not hold the Christian faith, says Constantine had nothing to do with the formation of the canon.
The earliest surviving list that matches today’s 27 books exactly is from Athanasius’s festal letter of 367.
The Muratorian Fragment reflects the list used in the Rome area at the end of the second century. This is the majority view; some (Sundberg, Hahneman) argue for a later date.

Both the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of Judas were written later than the date most scholars give for the four Gospels. This is quite firm for the Gospel of Judas; for the Gospel of Thomas there is no consensus on its date and sources, and some scholars hold that it preserves early tradition.

The argument over the boundaries of the canon was real: Hebrews, Revelation, 2 Peter and others were questioned; the Syriac Peshitta New Testament originally had only 22 books; Luther placed four books in a secondary position.

God’s providence guided the church to recognize the books He had inspired. This is a judgment of faith. History can describe the process but can neither prove nor disprove the work of the Holy Spirit.
Perspectives Room
Is the canon an authority added later, or do the books carry authority in themselves?

items.h: The canon was a decision of the church in the third and fourth centuries, and the power and theological struggles of the time shaped the outcome. The biblical books did not necessarily have a sense of being “Scripture” at first; early Christianity was more diverse than it was later presented.

Michael Kruger argues that this sense of authority existed within Christianity very early: the apostles wrote with authority, the letters circulated among the churches, and the later lists recognized an existing reality.
The church did exercise judgment, those judgments went through disputes, and settling the books at the margins took several hundred years.

blocks.h: A God who is willing to speak
The premise of the canon is that God has spoken and that people can recognize it. The peak of the whole Old Testament is God entering history Himself and speaking through His Son.
God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son,

The criterion of apostolicity is rooted in Jesus’ own promise. He told the disciples beforehand that the Holy Spirit would remind them of everything He had said. The church’s test for a book was to ask whether it brings people back to this Lord, crucified and risen.
But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.
The risen Jesus Himself read the Old Testament this way: He pointed the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms to Himself. The center of the canon is a person, and His cross.
He said to them, “This is what I told you while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled.”

Today, read a passage from a Gospel, slowly and aloud. Imagine a fourth-century believer in Egypt receiving Athanasius’s letter and hearing this same passage read; then imagine a second-century believer in Rome. What you are hearing is the voice of the same Shepherd.
Meditate: Do I treat the Bible more like picking the passages I like, or am I willing to let this measuring rod measure me?

Prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for opening Your mouth to speak to people, and for speaking Your last and deepest word through Your Son. Thank You for keeping Your church through the long course of history. Holy Spirit, open my ears so that I recognize the voice of the Good Shepherd, obey Your word, and let Jesus reign in my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: a measuring rod is not for measuring other people. Measure yourself first today, and then talk about others.

Letting God be God and people be people: when you talk about the Apocrypha with Catholic and Orthodox friends, remember that in the essentials there is unity and in the peripheral matters grace; there is no need to fight for a win.
Jesus is my example: as He read the Scriptures, I learn to read them: looking for Him everywhere.

blocks.h: This week: look over the table of contents of the New Testament, choose a short letter you have never finished (for example Philemon or Jude), read it through in one sitting, and write down one sentence from it that makes you think of Christ.
Pass it on: Have you ever heard that “the Bible was picked by a Roman emperor”? What ancient sources do you think one would need to check to find out whether that claim is right?
Quiz

quiz.q: What was the relationship between the Council of Nicaea (325) and the canon?
o: The emperor chose the 27 books on the spot
Neither the council records nor the eyewitnesses mention the council deciding on a list of books
It burned all the other gospels
quiz.e: The story of the books falling off the altar comes from a document of about the ninth century, and Voltaire made it widely known.

quiz.q: Who produced the earliest surviving list that matches today’s 27 books exactly?
o: Athanasius, AD 367
Marcion, about AD 140
Luther, 16th century
quiz.e: Athanasius’s thirty-ninth festal letter lists exactly the same 27 books.

quiz.q: Which of these was not a question the early church commonly asked in judging books?
o: Does it come from an apostle or someone connected with the apostles?
Is it widely used by churches in different places?
Was it approved by the Roman emperor?
quiz.e: The commonly cited criteria are apostolicity, catholicity and orthodoxy.

units.title: Archaeology and the Old Testament
units.sub: An enemy’s victory stele bears the words “House of David”; a tiny silver scroll carries the priestly blessing. What has archaeology dug up, and what can it never dig up?

share.v: Truth springs out of the earth. Righteousness has looked down from heaven.

blocks.h: In 1979, in an ancient tomb southwest of Jerusalem’s Old City, an archaeological team found two rolled-up pieces of silver thinner than a cigarette. It took specialists years to unroll them carefully and read them. Engraved on them was a blessing that many churches still speak over their people at the close of worship today.

These two silver scrolls were written around 600 BC, on the eve of Jerusalem’s fall to Babylon, and they are the oldest fragments of Old Testament text known so far. The city was destroyed and the temple burned, yet the words of the blessing stayed in the ground for more than two and a half thousand years.
Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.
Five pieces of evidence from the ground

The Israel Stele: discovered by Flinders Petrie at Thebes in Egypt in 1896, this is the victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah from about 1208 BC. Most scholars read line 27 as “Israel,” written with the sign that marks “a group of people.” It is the earliest mention of Israel in writing outside the Bible.

The Tel Dan Stele: this fragmentary Aramaic inscription came out of the ground in northern Israel in 1993 and 1994, and it most likely dates to the time of the Aramean king Hazael (9th century BC). The man who set it up boasts of defeating the king of Israel and a king of the “House of David.” Most scholars regard this as the first clear mention of the Davidic dynasty outside the Bible.

The Mesha Stele: discovered in 1868 at Dibon in present-day Jordan and now held in the Louvre. King Mesha of Moab tells how he broke free from the control of the house of Omri. It is the other side’s account of the same affair found in 2 Kings 3, though the two tell the outcome in opposite ways.

The Lachish reliefs and the Sennacherib Prism: in 701 BC the great Assyrian army invaded Judah. Huge reliefs from the palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, picture the capture of Lachish. The Assyrian annals record the taking of 46 fortified cities of Judah and say that Hezekiah was shut up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage,” yet they do not say that this city was taken.

Hezekiah’s Tunnel: 2 Kings 20:20 mentions how Hezekiah “made the pool, and the conduit, and brought water into the city.” Radiometric dating published in the journal Nature in 2003 placed this rock tunnel, about 533 meters long, in Iron Age II, and it also overturned the claim that the tunnel was built in the 2nd century BC.

In a courtroom, the weightiest words are often the ones the opposing side let slip. The man who raised the Tel Dan Stele was Israel’s enemy, the author of the Mesha Stele was a vassal king who rebelled against Israel, and Sennacherib was the invader who came to besiege the city. None of them had any motive to speak well of the Bible, and yet they left the same cast of names in stone.
The hardest question: the Exodus and the conquest of Canaan

Here we have to be honest. Egyptian records so far make no direct mention of a mass departure of Israelites, and the wilderness route has left no agreed remains. As for the destruction layer of Jericho’s walls, Kathleen Kenyon dated it to about 1550 BC; in 1990 Bryant Wood argued for redating it to about 1400 BC, and Piotr Bienkowski promptly answered him; the 1995 carbon dating results leaned toward the 17th to 16th centuries BC, which gives more support to Kenyon.

items.h: The Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen argues that the Old Testament’s cultural details and chronological setting broadly fit, and that a lack of direct evidence is not counterevidence. James Hoffmeier gathers the Egyptian background and concludes that the Exodus tradition has a real foundation. Kitchen acknowledges that Jericho’s 13th-century layers have eroded away and can no longer be found.

The archaeologists Israel Finkelstein and Neil Silberman argue that archaeology finds no trace of a mass departure and a swift conquest, that the cultural details of these narratives largely reflect the 7th century BC, and that early Israel developed mainly from within Canaan itself.

Some, following 1 Kings 6:1, place the Exodus at about the 15th century BC; others place it at about the 13th century BC. Both believe the event really happened and read the archaeological data differently. This hall sets them side by side and does not rule between them.

Many scholars also think that a smaller group went through an escape from Egypt, and that its memory later became the tradition of all Israel. A 2015 interdisciplinary volume shows how wide this discussion is.

blocks.h: The critics’ main point is that the present data can hardly support the traditional reading of a large-scale, short-term conquest. Evangelical scholars respond that the data are fragmentary, that ancient nomadic groups rarely left traces in the first place, and that Joshua 11:13 says only one city, Hazor, was burned. Both sides have a point, and this question has not been settled.

The reading of physical evidence can change too. In line 31 of the Mesha Stele, André Lemaire read “House of David” in 1994; in 2019 Finkelstein, Na’aman and Römer proposed reading instead the name of Balak, the Moabite king in the Bible; other scholars still hold that the damage is too heavy to decide. On the Tel Dan Stele, BYTDWD has no word divider in the middle, and some have argued it is a place name or a divine name, though most scholars do not accept this.

A minority has also questioned the date of the silver scrolls (Renz and Röllig do not rule out a later one). In 2004 a University of Southern California team re-examined them with new imaging and supported a date before the fall of Jerusalem. The scrolls show that this blessing was already in circulation then; they are not enough to show that the whole book of Numbers or the Pentateuch had already been completed.
What was actually dug up, and what is our own inference? Let’s mark them separately.

Israel already existed in Canaan by the end of the 13th century BC; Assyria invaded Judah in 701 BC and besieged Lachish; and Hezekiah paid tribute to Assyria. Writing and images from outside the Bible bear witness to all of this.

Radiometric dating places Hezekiah’s Tunnel in Iron Age II. The dating itself cannot write the name of the project’s owner; the link with Hezekiah is a historical judgment made by bringing in 2 Kings.

That the Tel Dan Stele’s BYTDWD means “House of David” is the mainstream reading at present, with a minority dissenting. It shows that a dynasty named after David existed by the 9th century BC; it does not confirm every episode of David’s life in Samuel.
The silver scrolls were written around 600 BC and are the oldest fragments of Old Testament text. The mainstream supports this date, and a minority of scholars question it.

On the scale, date and route of the Exodus and the conquest of Canaan, archaeology has reached no settled conclusion. The dispute over Jericho’s date continues to this day, and recent excavations have also reopened discussion of occupation there in the Late Bronze Age.

The God of the Bible acts in real times and real places, which is why the Bible dares to set itself within a history that can be checked. Archaeology can support or challenge the setting of a narrative, but it cannot prove the works of God, and it cannot take the place of faith.
The faithful God speaks in history
The enemy on the Tel Dan Stele thought he had finished off the “House of David.” But God had promised David this:
Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.

The stele was smashed and built into a wall. This house, too, looked as though its throne had been cut off, and Jerusalem later fell. Hundreds of years on, an angel told a young woman in Nazareth that the child she would bear was a descendant of David, and the road He walked led to the cross and the empty tomb.

He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom.

The line on the silver scroll, “Yahweh make his face to shine on you,” finds its deepest answer in Christ. Because He bore our sins, the face of God is no longer a judgment we dread, and that light has shone into human hearts.
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

Find someone, or stand in front of a mirror, and slowly read Numbers 6:24-26 aloud once. Imagine someone in 600 BC wearing these few lines on their body and walking through a Jerusalem about to be engulfed by war.

Meditate: Is my faith propped up by the next archaeology headline, or by the Lord who is faithful in history and rose from the dead? When I meet a question that has no answer yet, do I dare to lay it honestly before Him?

Pray: Faithful God, You act in real history, and You step into my real life too. Please make Your face to shine on me, help me face hard questions honestly, and let me rest securely in Your promises in Christ. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: I believe the Bible, and I won’t exaggerate on its behalf. If something can’t be verified, I say it can’t be verified. That is what honoring the truth looks like.
Humility overcomes pride: scholars change their minds, and I misread things too. I lay down the debater’s “I have to win” and let God be God.

Moving from a temporary perspective to an eternal one: the empires’ victory steles are shattered, and God’s promises are still standing. Whatever is making me anxious today, I set it back against that long a span of time.

blocks.h: This week: go to the British Museum or Israel Museum website, look at photos of the Lachish reliefs or the silver scrolls, and pass one fact and its related Scripture on to a brother or sister. Then use Numbers 6:24-26 to bless someone.

Pass it on: A religious book that dares to write down people, places and wars for anyone to check: do you find that interesting? How do you see the relationship between that book and what archaeologists have dug up?
Quiz

quiz.q: Why does the Tel Dan Stele matter?
o: Solomon set it up with his own hands
It is most likely the first clear mention of the “House of David” outside the Bible
It confirms every detail of David’s life
quiz.e: The stele was set up by an Aramean enemy. Most scholars read “House of David,” but it shows only that the dynasty existed.

quiz.q: On the archaeology of the Exodus, which statement is the most honest?
o: There is no direct archaeological evidence yet, and scholars differ in how they read the data
Archaeology has fully confirmed it
Archaeology has fully refuted it
quiz.e: The lack of direct evidence is a fact. What that means is read from several positions and remains undecided.

quiz.q: Where does the text on the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls come from?
o: The Ten Commandments
Psalm 23
The priestly blessing of Numbers 6
quiz.e: The scrolls were written around 600 BC, and their content is the blessing of Numbers 6:24-26.

units.title: Archaeology and the New Testament
units.sub: A heel bone with the nail still in it. How far can stones testify for the Gospels, and where do they stop?

share.v: it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.

blocks.h: In 1968, at a building site north of Jerusalem, workers dug up several Jewish burial caves. On one of the bone boxes a name was carved: Yehohanan.

Inside the box was a human heel bone with an iron nail, about 11.5 centimeters long, still driven through it. This is physical evidence of a first-century man who was crucified, and to this day it is the least disputed example.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
Names carved in stone

The Pilate Stone: found in June 1961 by an Italian archaeological team in the ancient theater at Caesarea; the stone had been reused by later people as a step. The inscription is damaged, and as reconstructed it reads Pilate, “prefect” of Judea. Pilate was already known from Josephus, Philo and Tacitus, so his existence does not depend on this stone; its value is that it preserves the title used at the time, praefectus (prefect), which can be compared with the later title “procurator” used by Tacitus.

The Caiaphas ossuary: in 1990 construction south of Jerusalem uncovered a family tomb. A beautifully made bone box bears, twice, the inscription “Joseph son of Caiaphas” or a similar spelling. Josephus records that the full name of the high priest was Joseph Caiaphas. Many scholars accept the identification, while others (such as Horbury) raise questions: the spelling is not exactly the same, and no mention is made of the title of high priest.

The Gallio inscription: nine fragments from Delphi, part of a letter from the Roman emperor Claudius written around AD 52, mention the proconsul Gallio. Acts 18:12 says Paul was brought before him for judgment, and this has become an important fixed point for constructing Paul’s chronology.

In court there is a kind of witness who does not know the defendant and does not care about the case, but happens to remember what the shops on that street were called that day. This witness will not plead for the defendant, yet can tell the judge: the street this person describes is real. Archaeology is mostly this kind of witness.
Places that were found

The Pool of Siloam: in the autumn of 2004, workers repairing a sewer dug into stone steps. The archaeologists Shukron and Reich recognized a large pool from the Second Temple period, about 69 meters wide, with coins from the time of Alexander Jannaeus in the plaster. This pool is often regarded as the place where the blind man washed his eyes in John 9. But in 2023 the Israeli archaeologist Nahshon Szanton proposed in ‘Atiqot that the true Pool of Siloam was a different pool a few hundred feet to the north. That there were large pools at the southern end of first-century Jerusalem is certain; which one was Siloam is still under discussion.

The Pool of Bethesda: John 5 says the pool was near the Sheep Gate and had five porticoes. In the nineteenth century scholars found large pools in the area of today’s Church of St. Anne, and the 1964 excavation confirmed two large pools, the dividing wall between them, and the remains of a later Roman healing sanctuary. The location is considered a fairly good match, but how the five porticoes were arranged and what they were used for at the time are still discussed.

Nazareth: in December 2009 the Israel Antiquities Authority found a small house from the early Roman period, with two rooms, a courtyard, a cistern cut into the rock, and fragments of the limestone vessels commonly used by Jews. The director, Yardenna Alexandre, thought it was probably a typical simple dwelling of the time. Ken Dark has also studied another first-century house at the nearby Sisters of Nazareth Convent and published a paper on it, though the title of his own article is also a question. There is no evidence showing which house, if either, belonged to Jesus’ family.
The nail of the cross

Early reports held that Yehohanan’s heel bones in both feet were pierced by a single nail and that his arms were also nailed to the crossbeam. In 1985 Zias and Sekeles reexamined the remains and corrected this: there was only one heel bone, and the “nail marks” on the arms are unreliable; he may have had his arms tied to the crossbeam. This correction is just what archaeological work ought to look like. There is also an Italian case from Gavello published in 2018, with a perforation but no nail, which scholars call only a possible case.
Evidence we do not use

The ossuary inscribed “James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus” caused a sensation when it was announced in 2002. The Israel Antiquities Authority then accused someone of forging part of the inscription. In 2012 the judge found the defendants not guilty of forgery, and at the same time explained that this does not mean the inscription is genuine, which has to be left for the future to decide. We do not treat it as evidence.

In 2018 Israeli scholars published a small bronze ring found at Herodium, engraved with “Pilate.” The name is not unique, and reports said only that it is “possibly” connected with the governor, so it cannot be taken as firm evidence.
Let’s take the claims one at a time and mark how certain each is.
The Pilate Stone (1961) is a first-century inscription that preserves the name of Pilate and the title of prefect. The inscription is damaged, and some letters are reconstructed.
Yehohanan’s heel bone (1968) is physical evidence of a first-century Jew who was crucified.
The Caiaphas ossuary belonged to the high priest of the Gospels. Most scholars accept this, and some raise questions.
The pool discovered in 2004 is the Pool of Siloam of John 9. This is the common identification, and recently there have been alternative proposals.
Whether the inscription on the James ossuary is genuine. The court neither found it forged nor found it genuine, and scholars remain divided. This unit does not use it.

These discoveries support the claim that the Gospels describe a real time and place, but they cannot prove that Jesus is the Son of God or that He rose from the dead. Those are matters of testimony and faith, not something a spade can dig up.
Perspectives Room
There are different assessments of what archaeology means for the credibility of the Gospels.

items.h: The place names, people and customs of the Gospels repeatedly match excavated evidence, which suggests the authors were close to the events. Siloam, Bethesda, Pilate and others do not look like inventions.

Accurate local color does not mean every event happened. A historical novel can also get the streets right. Archaeology is not evidence exclusive to the Gospels either; the same kind of method also supports many other ancient accounts.
Archaeology can rule out the simple view that the Gospels are pure legend, but it walks with us only as far as the door of the tomb and stops there.

blocks.h: He entered a history that can be checked

Luke says at the very start that he is writing about things that can be investigated. The Christian faith does not place salvation at the edge of a myth; it fixes the death of the Savior in the term of office of a named Roman official.

Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
God did not send a representative. He Himself became a man who lived in a humble house in a small village.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
Yehohanan’s heel bone tells us how real the cross was. The risen Jesus did not ask Thomas to believe an abstract idea; He held out His hands, with the marks of the nails.
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.

Open your palm and gently press the fingers of your other hand into the center of it. Think about that 11.5-centimeter iron nail. Jesus is not a distant concept; His body was once nailed to wood, for you.
Meditate: Is my faith more like collecting an antique, or like meeting a living Lord with the marks of the nails in His hands?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, You did not live in a myth. You entered our history, walked our streets, and suffered a real nailing. Thank You for being pierced for my sins and for rising from the dead. Move me from only wanting to see evidence to saying to You: My Lord and my God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: this book is set in real history, and it deserves to be set in my real life too.
People matter more than tasks: other people will not read archaeological reports, but they will see how I treat them. My life is also a testimony that can be checked.
Humility overcomes pride: where something is uncertain, say it is uncertain. Evidence like the James ossuary, however moving, is not used.

blocks.h: This week: read John 9, find the Siloam area of Jerusalem on a map, then write one sentence of your own “once… now…” testimony and tell one person.

Pass it on: If the place names and official titles in an ancient book are repeatedly dug up and found to match, would that make you more willing to read it? What other tests do you think it still has to pass?
Quiz

quiz.q: What is the main value of the Pilate Stone (1961)?
o: It proved for the first time that Pilate existed
It preserves a contemporary inscription and his title of “prefect”
It records the course of Jesus’ trial
quiz.e: Josephus, Philo and Tacitus had already mentioned Pilate; the inscription’s value lies in the title used at the time.

quiz.q: What does Yehohanan’s heel bone tell us?
o: Physical evidence of a first-century man who was crucified
Where Jesus’ tomb is
That everyone who was crucified was nailed by the hands
quiz.e: It is physical evidence; even whether his arms were nailed has been corrected from early reports by scholars.

quiz.q: Why does this unit not use the James ossuary as evidence?
o: Because the court ruled it a forgery
Because it has gone missing
Because the court did not find it forged but also did not find it genuine, so its authenticity is undecided
quiz.e: The judge stated plainly that the not-guilty verdict does not mean the inscription is genuine. Doubtful evidence is not used, however moving it is.

units.title: Messianic Prophecy
units.sub: A key older than Jesus. Was it really cast for this door? Jewish readers and Christians each have their own way of reading.

share.v: He said to them, “This is what I told you while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled.”

blocks.h: More than a hundred years before Jesus was born, a passage about a suffering servant had already been copied onto a leather scroll and stored in a cave by the Dead Sea.

This is the Great Isaiah Scroll, about 7.3 meters long, with 54 columns in all. Judging by the handwriting, it was copied around 150–100 BC; the calibrated carbon-dating range is 356–103 BC. Chapter 53 is right there on it.

The wonder doesn’t stop there. In the very same passage Christians read about Jesus, while many Jewish readers read about their own people’s thousand-year-old scars. Both have read it with tears streaming down their faces.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
First, separate two questions

When people discuss prophecy, two questions often get tangled together. First, was this text written before the events? Second, does it refer to Jesus? The first can be checked against the manuscripts. The second depends on interpretation, and interpretation is contested.

You dig an old key out of a drawer, and an appraiser tells you it was cast more than a hundred years ago. That only proves the key is old enough; it says nothing yet about which door it opens. You have to go and try it. And after you try it you still have to ask: was this door designed for the key from the start, or did someone shave down the frame to fit it? The Dead Sea Scrolls answer the first half of the question. The second half is a journey we have to make ourselves.
Isaiah 53: who is the servant?
In Jewish tradition this question has never had just one answer.

items: The servant is the nation of Israel: Rabbi Rashi (1040–1105) said that this prophet habitually addresses all Israel as one person. This was no new medieval idea. Around AD 248 the Christian scholar Origen recorded that a Jewish scholar told him this prophecy referred to the whole nation.

The servant is the Messiah: the Aramaic Targum Jonathan renders Isaiah 52:13 directly as “my servant the Messiah.” The Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b, also cites 53:4 when discussing the names of the Messiah.
The servant is the community of the righteous: some rabbis applied parts of the passage to righteous people who willingly suffer.

blocks.h: So both statements, “Jews have always read it only as Israel” and “ancient Jews all read it as the Messiah,” are too simple.

items.h: The book of Isaiah says more than once, in plain words, that the servant is Israel (41:8; 49:3). A nation despised, a nation from whom people hide their faces: set in the history of Jewish exile and persecution, every word carries blood and tears, including the suffering Christians themselves inflicted on them.

53:8 says the servant was cut off “for the disobedience of my people,” so the servant and “my people” seem to be two different parties. The servant of 49:5-6 is to bring Jacob back to God, and so does not appear to be the same as all of Jacob. The silent endurance of 53:7 and the innocence of 53:9 are also hard to fit onto any actual nation.

Most critical scholars place this chapter back in the exile: the servant is the exiled community of that time, or some particular figure. Some scholars, such as Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Brettler, hold that its original meaning was not to foretell the Messiah; others, such as Martin Hengel, hold that individualizing and even messianic readings were already budding before Christ.

blocks.h: Three other frequently cited passages

items: Micah 5:2: a ruler comes from Bethlehem. The Targum mentions the Messiah here too, which shows this was no Christian invention. But the verses right after it, 5:5-6, speak of resisting Assyria, and on that basis Jewish readers point out that this ruler’s achievements are still unfulfilled.

Zechariah 9:9: a lowly king comes riding on a donkey. Talmud Sanhedrin 98a records that R. Alexandri said that if Israel is worthy, the Messiah will come on the clouds of heaven, and if unworthy, riding on a donkey. Christians for their part notice that Jesus entered the city this way on purpose, so this does not count as a coincidence beyond His control.

Psalm 22:16: this verse turns on how one word is read. The Masoretic Text has “like a lion, my hands and my feet”; the Septuagint has “they pierced,” and the Chinese Union Version translates along the lines of the latter. A fragment from Nahal Hever seems to support the verbal reading, but both the handwriting and the root are disputed. Notably, the New Testament quotes other verses of Psalm 22 yet does not quote this one.

blocks.h: Daniel’s seventy weeks

Daniel 9:24-27 is one of the hardest prophecies of all. Tradition offers at least three paths. One: it points to Antiochus IV and the persecution of the second century BC, and the anointed one is the high priest Onias III. Two: it points to the death of Christ and the destruction of the temple in AD 70. Three: the first sixty-nine weeks reach to Christ, and the seventieth week is still in the future. Rashi, for his part, held that the anointed one who is cut off is King Agrippa, with “anointed” here simply a term for kings and nobles. Evangelical scholars hold differing positions. We lay these side by side without ruling among them, and we do not calculate any date from this passage.
Why we don’t use “probability calculations”

In 1958 the American mathematics and astronomy teacher Peter Stoner estimated in Science Speaks that the probability of one man fulfilling eight prophecies is 1 in 10<sup>17</sup>, a figure that has since been widely repeated. The problems are large. Each prophecy’s probability rests on a subjective estimate. The eight are not independent of one another (being born in Bethlehem raises the likelihood of entering Jerusalem), yet they are multiplied as if they were independent events. Some of the events are things a person could deliberately carry out. And the eight were picked after the fact. Critics such as Bradley Bowen have pointed out the problem of dependence. A pretty number can’t buy trust. This unit does not use this kind of argument.
A challenge: did the Gospels make up stories to match the prophecies?

Skeptics ask: since the New Testament writers knew the Old Testament so well, might they have written Old Testament lines into the life of Jesus? This question deserves a serious look. The scrolls can establish that the Old Testament text came first, but on their own they cannot establish the Gospel accounts. John also admits frankly that the disciples didn’t understand at the time: “when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered” (John 12:16). The Christian response is that if you were making it up, no one would choose a crucified Messiah. In his second-century dialogue with Justin, the Jew Trypho found the cross the hardest thing of all to accept.
Let’s look at how old the key is and where the key goes as two separate matters.

The Great Isaiah Scroll was copied before Christ, with chapter 53 complete. It broadly agrees with the Masoretic Text, and it also has more than 2,600 variants large and small; at 53:11, for example, it has the added word “light” (as does the Septuagint).
Jewish tradition holds several interpretations side by side, including “the servant is Israel” and “the servant is the Messiah”; the former is already on record as early as Origen’s time (about 248).
Scholars are still discussing whether Isaiah 53 already had a messianic, suffering reading in Judaism before Christ.
The original reading of Psalm 22:16, “like a lion” or “they pierced,” is still debated.
There is no agreed answer on the calculation and referent of Daniel 9:24-27.

That these passages find their deepest fulfillment in Jesus is a Christian judgment of faith. It has textual and historical reasons in its support, yet it cannot be proved by probability formulas or textual research alone.
A very long letter from God

Prophecy teaches us more than God’s ability to foretell. It lets us see that God is willing to spend hundreds and thousands of years keeping His word, and willing to let people understand it slowly. That is how the risen Jesus, on the road to Emmaus, walked with two disappointed people and reread the Scriptures with them.
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
The Ethiopian eunuch once asked this same question, and the Christian answer of two thousand years begins from here too.
The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?” Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.

People expected a king on a warhorse. The King God sent rode a donkey and hung on a tree. No one would have imagined saving the world this way, which is why Paul admits it is a stumbling block. Yet it is exactly here that Isaiah’s words become personal grace: the wounds He received were for me.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds.
Read Isaiah 53:3-6 slowly, twice. The second time, whenever you reach “we,” “our” or “us,” put your own name there.
Meditate: are my expectations of Jesus more like a king on a warhorse, or a king on a donkey? When His ways don’t match what I expect, how do I respond?

Prayer: Faithful Lord, from ancient times until now Your word has never failed. Thank You for being pierced for my transgressions and crushed for my iniquities. Make my heart burn for Your word, and give me gentleness to respect those who read it differently from me. In the name of Jesus, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: read prophecy in its context, and don’t lean on inflated numbers to prop God up.
Jesus is my example: He rode into the city on a donkey and laid aside all show of power. When I am the one with the upper hand, I too can choose gentleness.

People matter more than tasks: when I meet Jewish friends, first remember the wounds they have carried, and respect their reading as well. Winning a debate over a verse can’t compare with winning someone’s trust.

blocks.h: This week: find a quiet time to read Isaiah 52:13–53:12, then Luke 24:13-35, and write down one sentence beginning “What moved me most was…” and one beginning “What I still want to ask is…”
Pass it on: if a piece of writing was written several hundred years before an event, how would you judge whether it is really talking about that event, or whether later readers read it in?
Quiz

quiz.q: What is the Great Isaiah Scroll’s most direct contribution to the question of prophecy?
o: It shows that the text of Isaiah 53 is older than Jesus
It shows that all Jews read it as the Messiah
It calculates the probability of Jesus fulfilling prophecy
quiz.e: It can establish that the text came before Christ; whom it points to still requires interpretation.

quiz.q: Which statement about Jewish interpretation of Isaiah 53 is most accurate?
o: The reading “the servant is Israel” only appeared in the Middle Ages
Jewish tradition has different readings: the nation, the righteous, the Messiah and others
Jewish tradition never discusses this passage
