quiz.e: Origen recorded the national reading around 248, and the Targum and the Talmud also contain readings connected with the Messiah.

quiz.q: Why doesn’t this unit use calculations like “1 in 10 to the 17th power”?
o: Because prophecy has nothing to do with numbers
Because probability is an unspiritual discipline
Because each probability rests on an estimate, and the items are not independent of one another
quiz.e: Multiplying dependent events as though they were independent produces a misleading number.

units.title: The Historical Details of Acts
units.sub: Did Luke get an official’s title wrong? A stone from a city gate came to his defense. But how far can accurate detail take us?

share.v: But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness. For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.

blocks.h: Acts 17 contains an official title that some early critics thought Luke had gotten wrong, because the word could not be found in any Greek literature known at the time.

The word is politarchēs, rendered “rulers of the city” in the English Bible. Later, when the Vardar Gate of Thessalonica was torn down in 1876, an inscription on it turned out to carry exactly this title. It is kept in the British Museum today. Several more inscriptions have turned up since, most of them in the region of Macedonia.
When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also,
The standard Luke set for himself

Right at the start Luke explains his method: he has investigated carefully and will write “in order.” This is how ancient historians typically opened their works. Scholars mostly discuss Acts within the range of ancient historical writing, though some, such as Richard Pervo, think it is closer to the style of a novel.

it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus;that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.

Suppose you want to tell whether a friend’s travel story is firsthand or copied from the internet. You listen for the small things: does he know which way the one-way street runs, which night-market stall is closed on Mondays? Luke’s book has this kind of “closed on Mondays” detail. But accurate detail shows at most that he knows his way around. Whether he remembered every event correctly still has to be checked.
Small things Luke got right

items: The “politarchs” of Thessalonica: Inscriptions show that Thessalonica really did have officials of this kind. They span the second century BC to the third century AD, and in Augustus’ time the city had five of them, which fits the plural used in Acts.

The “proconsul” of Cyprus: From 22 BC Cyprus was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul, and Luke calls Sergius Paulus a proconsul (13:7). An inscription found at Soloi on Cyprus’s north coast mentions a “proconsul Paulus,” but its date-line is disputed (read as year 10 or 13 of Claudius, about AD 50–54, and possibly added later) and it gives only the name Paulus. A fragmentary decree from Kythraia is restored by some as naming a proconsul Quintus Sergius [Paullus], but that restoration is also contested. Whether either is the same man can only be called possible.
Gallio of Corinth: A letter of the emperor Claudius found at Delphi (around AD 52) mentions the proconsul Gallio. This fits Acts 18:12 and is a key anchor for building Paul’s chronology.
Figures of Judean politics: Felix and his Jewish wife Drusilla, the succession of Festus, and the high priest Ananias can all be set beside the record of Josephus.

blocks.h: The shipwreck passage is especially famous. In 1848 the Scottish yachtsman and student of ancient seafaring James Smith published The Voyage and Shipwreck of St. Paul, which studied Acts 27 against the Mediterranean’s sea conditions and ancient ships. Colin Hemer later noted that Luke records the sailors’ fear of the Syrtis shoals and the sounding of the depth in the bay off Malta in a layman’s vocabulary, just like an onlooker aboard the ship.
The skeptics’ serious reasons
Let’s fairly hear three reasons from the other side.

items: The date of Theudas: Acts 5:36 has Gamaliel mention Theudas in the AD 30s, and before Judas the Galilean. But the Theudas in Josephus appears under the procurator Fadus in the time of Claudius (around AD 44–46). Some propose that there was another Theudas of the same name, some think Luke made a mistake, and some think he misread Josephus. There is no settled answer at present.

Differences from Paul’s letters: Philipp Vielhauer argued that Acts conflicts with Paul’s letters on the law, natural theology and other matters. Recent scholarship mostly holds that the two are closer than he said, but real differences of detail remain, for example in Paul’s relationship with Peter and James.

The Asiarchs: The Asiarchs of 19:31 are often cited as an example of local detail. Stephan Witetschek, however, argues that such details reflect Luke’s own era in Ephesus more than Paul’s, and are not necessarily the same as the situation in Paul’s time.

blocks.h: None of these three is a small matter. The first remains unresolved to this day.
Date and authorship

Most scholars date Acts to about AD 80–90, and some argue for earlier. In 2006 Pervo argued for composition in the early second century, holding that Luke used Josephus and Paul’s letters. Andrew Gregory, in a 2016 review, judged that the case for Luke’s use of these sources carries some weight but does not necessarily lead to the second century. Critical scholars are divided over whether the author is the physician Luke of church tradition, though most still think the author knew Paul. The “we” passages in the book are key evidence, and some regard them as a literary device.

items.h: Hemer, Craig Keener and others hold that by the standards of Greco-Roman historiography Acts has considerable value as a historical source; Keener devotes four large volumes to the evidence.
Pervo and others hold that the author’s theological and apologetic aims drive the narrative, and that accurate local color does not guarantee the events themselves.
Most commentators accept that Luke was an ancient historian, but also that, like every ancient historian, he selected, condensed and composed speeches, so each case must be judged on its own.

blocks.h: Let’s separate “accurate local color” from “all the events are reliable.”
The word “politarch” (politarchēs) is attested by many inscriptions, including some from Thessalonica.
The Delphi inscription mentions the proconsul Gallio, dated to about AD 52, which fits the person in Acts 18:12.
By the standards of ancient historical writing, Acts has considerable value as a historical source. This is the judgment of many scholars, and important dissent remains.
The date of composition (first century or early second century) and the identity of the author are still under discussion; the problem of Theudas is unresolved.

William Ramsay (1851–1939) began under the influence of the Tübingen school, then after fieldwork came to hold Luke in high regard. But his later popular apologetic works have drawn criticism from scholars, and the story that “an archaeologist came to faith because of this” is often overstated.

Luke’s seriousness about what can be checked gives us reason to take seriously what he records that cannot be checked, such as miracles. But this does not prove that the miracles happened. Whether to believe remains a decision of faith.
God works at places with an address

Many religious stories take place “long, long ago.” The story of Acts has official titles, provinces and city gates. Paul dared to tell a king that these things were not done in a corner. God’s faithfulness shows itself in history, in these places whose addresses can be looked up.

But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness. For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.

These officials, sea conditions and inscriptions are only the outer edge. The whole book revolves around one center, something the disciples were willing to go to prison for, to be flogged for, even to die for.
This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses.

A title on a city gate can be dug up, but the resurrection you and I have to face in person. Paul did not rest his faith on inscriptions. He staked everything on Christ, and he said honestly that without the resurrection everything collapses.
If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.

Open to Acts 27 and slowly read through the whole shipwreck. Notice verse 29: they cast four anchors and wished for daylight. Think about what you are waiting for daylight to bring in your own night right now.
Meditate: Does my faith have an “address”? Can I name the time, the place and the people when I speak of what God has done in my life?

Pray: Lord of history, thank You that You do not work in a fog. You have entered our cities and our shipwrecks. Thank You that Your Son truly died and truly rose again. Reign also in my own streets and alleys, and let me live out a witness that can be checked. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: Believe it, and examine it. Luke himself “traced” everything carefully, so let’s not be lazy when we read.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry: The church in Acts began with prayer and being of one mind. Ministry came later as the fruit.
Changing our lives: Let my witness have an address. How others see me treat my coworkers and my family is how they check the historical details of the book that is me.

blocks.h: This week: Spend a week reading Acts 16–19 (Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus). Mark Paul’s route on a map, and write down one question you would like to dig into.

Pass it on: When you judge whether an ancient book or a news story can be trusted, what do you look at? If the author gets even the small, checkable details right, are you more willing to believe him?
Quiz

quiz.q: What does the example of the “politarch” show?
o: Every event in Acts has been proven by archaeology
Luke was quite familiar with the details of local institutions
All the scholars who criticize Acts have changed their minds
quiz.e: It supports the view that Luke knew local conditions well, but it cannot by itself prove the whole book.

quiz.q: What does this unit say about Theudas in Acts 5:36?
o: There is a tension in dating with Josephus’ account, and there is no settled answer at present
There is no problem at all
It has been proven that Luke plagiarized
quiz.e: Josephus places Theudas in AD 44–46, while Gamaliel’s speech falls in the AD 30s. There are several proposed solutions, none settled.

quiz.q: What is the most that “accurate local color” can support?
o: All miracles have been confirmed by science
There is no need to think further about questions of faith
The author is a serious witness who knew the situation and deserves to be taken seriously
quiz.e: This makes Luke worth reading seriously, while the decision of faith still has to be faced by each person.

units.title: Does the Bible Contradict Itself?
units.sub: Some hard questions can be untangled, and some are still hanging in the air today. Faith is not afraid to lay them out on the table.

share.v: Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth.

blocks.h: On the cross where Jesus was nailed there was a sign. All four Gospels record what it said, and all four write it differently.
Mark has only “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Matthew adds “THIS IS” and “JESUS.” Luke has “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.” John has “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

The church plainly had the chance to make them uniform. In the second century AD, Tatian actually did edit the four Gospels into a single book, the Diatessaron, and it circulated in parts of the Syriac-speaking church for about three centuries. In the end the church returned to four separate books and handed them down, differences and all.
Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
A difference is not a contradiction

Strictly speaking, a contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true at the same time. “They have two children” and “They have a daughter” sound different, yet both can be right. So when you run into a hard passage, the first step is to ask: do these two places really exclude each other, or have I been reading them as the same kind of document?

Think of one wedding. The photographer’s album, the bride’s mother’s memories and the best man’s speech will each keep some things and leave out others. If all three matched word for word, you would start to suspect someone had copied. But don’t push the comparison too far: selection can explain differences, but it cannot smooth away every difference.
Five keys

items: Genre: the exaggeration of poetry, the general rules of Proverbs and the stories of parables can’t be read as courtroom transcripts.
Selective narration: John himself says Jesus did many other signs, “which are not written in this book” (John 20:30). Recording one angel does not necessarily deny a second.

Translation: Acts 9:7 says Paul’s companions were “hearing the sound,” while in the Chinese Union Version, the classic Chinese Bible, Acts 22:9 says they did not hear it clearly. The one Greek verb covers both hearing and understanding, so many modern translations also give 22:9 as “didn’t understand.”

Manuscripts: 2 Kings 8:26 says Ahaziah was 22 when he came to the throne, and 2 Chronicles 22:2 says 42. Some Septuagint manuscripts and the Syriac version also read 22 in 2 Chronicles. Many scholars see this as a problem from the copying process, and others have proposed different ways of counting.
Ancient writing habits: ancient biographies would compress, rearrange the order and focus on one person. Holding them to today’s news standards is like taking a temperature with a ruler.

blocks.h: Four examples

The two genealogies. From David to Joseph, Matthew 1 and Luke 3 are almost two separate lists, and they even differ on Joseph’s father (Jacob / Heli). In the third century AD, Julius Africanus proposed an explanation based on a man marrying his brother’s widow, and he admitted frankly that his account could not be corroborated. Another view holds that Luke records Mary’s family line, but her name does not appear in Luke’s list. To this day the question has no agreed answer.

The death of Judas. Matthew says he “hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5). Acts says “falling headlong, his body burst open” (Acts 1:18). The common harmonization goes like this: after he hanged himself the body fell, and each passage records one side of it. Bart Ehrman argues that the two passages also differ on who bought the field and why it was called the field of blood, so they shouldn’t be forced together. You can read both sides’ reasons for yourself and then judge.

The morning of the resurrection. How many women, one angel or two, still dark or after sunrise: all four accounts vary. Yet all four agree on this: the first day of the week, the women arrive first, the stone is already moved, and the tomb is empty.

Genesis 1 and 2. In chapter 1 the animals come before humans; 2:19 in the Chinese Union Version reads as if the beasts were made after the man. The NIV and ESV render this verse as God “had formed” them, while the KJV uses a simple past tense. Critical scholars mostly treat these as two sources. Richard Hess points out that, whatever the sources were, this double pattern of first surveying the whole and then focusing on one place is a deliberate literary arrangement, just like the genealogies in Genesis 4–5 and 10–11.
Two main ways of stating inerrancy
Evangelicals don’t all define “inerrancy” in exactly the same way, and scholars from different camps debate one another in public.

items.h: The 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy: the original manuscripts of the Bible are true in all they say, including statements of history and science; but round numbers, hyperbole and accounts without modern precision do not count as errors.

The Bible is completely reliable in its teaching on faith and life, while details of history and nature may carry human limitations. Article XII of the Chicago Statement explicitly rejects this limitation.

Michael Licona holds that the Bible is without error in all that it teaches, and he accepts the writing freedom of ancient biography. Lydia McGrew and others criticize this as conceding too much, while Craig Blomberg thinks the truth lies between the two.

blocks.h: Questions still hanging today

Mark 2:26 says David ate the show bread “at the time of Abiathar the high priest,” while 1 Samuel 21:1 names the priest as Ahimelech. Ehrman recalls writing a paper at Princeton Theological Seminary defending this verse, and his professor, Cullen Story, commented to the effect that perhaps Mark had simply made a mistake. This became a crack in his journey of faith. But by his own account, the decisive reason he finally left the faith was the problem of suffering.

Matthew 27:9 attributes to “Jeremiah the prophet” words close to Zechariah 11:12–13. There are several proposed solutions (such as a combined quotation, or citing under the name of the major prophet), and none of them satisfies everyone. We are willing to tell you exactly that: some of these questions are still being discussed by evangelical scholars themselves.
Sort the claims into levels, and you’ll know where the ground is firm and where the discussion is still going on.
The four Gospels record different wording for the sign on the cross, and “THE KING OF THE JEWS” appears in all four. Readers can open their Bibles and check for themselves.

Around AD 405, Augustine was already writing to Jerome about this kind of difficulty: where something in Scripture seemed contrary to truth, he would suspect a faulty manuscript, a translator who had missed the sense, or his own failure to understand. So the church has always known about these questions.
Many differences among the four Gospels can be accounted for by the writing conventions of ancient biography; evangelicals disagree on how far this method can be taken.
The relationship between the two genealogies, Mark 2:26 and Matthew 27:9 currently have no agreed solution. Some scholars consider them real errors or theological constructions.

The differences in the Bible have not shaken its core witness; the Bible is inspired by God and completely trustworthy. This is a judgment of faith. It has reasons supporting it, but it is not a conclusion that textual and historical research can prove on its own.
God dares to use four witnesses

God could easily have handed us one flawless official record. According to church tradition, the four Gospels came from a tax collector, a co-worker of Peter, a doctor and a fisherman, each speaking of the same Jesus in his own voice. There is real courage in this faithfulness: His word can stand up to word-by-word examination, and it invites us to come and examine it.
Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.

And on the one thing the Bible cares about most, none of the four is vague. This passage from Paul, which most scholars believe was written before the Gospels, points straight to the cross and the resurrection.

For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,

When the risen Christ met Thomas, who was full of doubt, He did not scold him for asking too many questions. He held out His nail-scarred hands. His answer is more than an explanation: it is Himself. The hard questions may not all be solved today, but you can already come before this One.
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.” Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Open Matthew 27:37, Mark 15:26, Luke 23:38 and John 19:19, and read the four signs side by side. Then stop on the title all four share: this One hung there for you.
Reflect: Is there a question about the Bible in my heart that I have never dared to ask? Am I afraid of the question itself, or of what I would have to face once I asked it?

Prayer: Faithful Lord, thank you that you are not afraid of my questions. Give me an honest heart that can examine and can also admit what I don’t yet understand. Above all, through the Bible, let me know Jesus, the One who died and rose again for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: precisely because it is the standard, I must handle it properly and never defend it by pulling words out of context.
Humility overcomes pride: being able to say “I don’t know the answer to this one yet” is where letting God be God begins, and it is a better witness than forcing an argument.
People matter more than tasks: when a friend brings up a hard question, he matters more than who wins the debate. First hear him out on why this question matters to him.

blocks.h: This week: choose one of the examples above, open the two passages yourself and compare them. Write one sentence beginning “What I see is…” and one beginning “What I still don’t understand is…”, then bring them to your small group or ask your pastor.
Pass it on: Is there a place in the Bible you’ve read or heard about that just doesn’t make sense to you? I’d really like to hear about it, and we could open it up and look at it together.
Quiz

quiz.q: Which of these comes closest to the strict definition of a “contradiction”?
o: Two accounts give different amounts of detail
Two statements cannot both be true at the same time
Two authors use different words
quiz.e: Differences of detail and wording don’t necessarily exclude each other; a contradiction means the two cannot both be true at the same time.

quiz.q: 2 Kings 8:26 and 2 Chronicles 22:2 give different ages for Ahaziah (22 / 42). What is the common explanation?
o: A problem in the copying tradition; some ancient versions also read 22 in 2 Chronicles
He reigned twice
The biblical authors couldn’t do arithmetic
quiz.e: Some Septuagint manuscripts and the Syriac version read 22, and it is mostly viewed as a problem in the copying tradition, though other ways of counting have also been proposed.

quiz.q: Faced with biblical difficulties still unsolved today, what attitude does this unit recommend?
o: Avoid talking about them so no one stumbles
Declare them all errors and stop reading
Honestly admit what is unsolved, keep examining and fix our eyes on Christ
quiz.e: 2 Timothy 2:15 calls us to handle the word properly; honesty glorifies God more than forcing an argument.

units.title: War and Cruelty in the Old Testament
units.sub: Some passages can keep you awake at night. This lesson will not smooth them over, and it will not tear them out either.

share.v: He who has seen me has seen the Father.

blocks.h: This sentence is printed right there in your Bible, and the one giving the order is Yahweh:
you shall save alive nothing that breathes

If you have ever reached this point and closed the book, you are far from alone. Richard Dawkins, in The God Delusion (2006), used passages like this to bring charges against the God of the Old Testament. The Osage scholar Robert Warrior has said that he reads Exodus through Canaanite eyes. Even Christopher Wright, an evangelical scholar who has spent his life teaching the Bible, admits that he has not yet found a good enough answer and that this still troubles him.
This lesson will lay the hardest passages on the table exactly as they stand, let each side speak in its strongest form, and tell you where things remain unsolved to this day.
First, read the whole text

The passages about the war in Canaan really are severe. At Jericho they killed “both man and woman, both young and old” (Joshua 6:21). Joshua “utterly destroyed all that breathed” (Joshua 10:40). The command Samuel relayed to Saul included even the “nursing baby” (1 Samuel 15:3). Any answer that says “it wasn’t really that bad” has to face these verses first.

These same texts also tell us that God waited more than four hundred years before acting (Genesis 15:13-16), that He promised to drive the inhabitants out “little by little” (Exodus 23:30), that the prostitute Rahab and her household were saved (Joshua 6:25), and that the opening of Judges goes on to list many Canaanites who were never driven out (Judges 1:28).

The morning after a big game, the headlines shout “sweep,” “bloodbath,” “wiped out,” and nobody calls the police. Ancient war records had language habits of their own too. The question is whether the exaggeration of a battle report can explain a command. That is exactly where the debate lies.
Three evangelical answers

Each of these is stated below in its strongest form. They exist side by side within the same faith, and the matter has not been settled. The evangelical scholar Charlie Trimm examined these approaches in his 2022 book and did not claim that the problem has been solved either.

items.h: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan argue that “leave no one” is the hyperbole of ancient war writing, that the Bible itself records many survivors, and that the weight of the command falls on expulsion and disarmament, so “genocide” is not an accurate word. Richard Hess and others think that most of the cities in the book were military strongholds. Weakness: in 1 Samuel 15, Saul is rebuked precisely for leaving someone alive, and the wording of the command is hard to read entirely as hyperbole.

items.n: The justice of God as Judge
items.h: Eugene Merrill and others accept the command literally, seeing it as a one-time judgment by the Lord of life on centuries of accumulated evil, one that cannot be repeated. William Lane Craig stresses that God has the right to give such a command, and has revised his view to say that the emphasis lies on expulsion, with only those who stayed behind to resist being struck down. Weakness: what sin have infants committed? And what would become of the people who carried out the order?

Eric Seibert and C. S. Cowles hold that we must distinguish the God depicted in the text from the true God. The Father whom Jesus revealed loves His enemies, and depictions that conflict with this are the understandings of ancient people shaped by their culture. Weakness: most evangelicals believe this weakens the authority of the Bible, and Jesus Himself accepted the Old Testament and spoke of a final judgment.

blocks.h: The critics’ strongest arguments

The philosopher Wesley Morriston argues that these passages are themselves strong evidence against biblical inerrancy; rather than say that God commanded the destruction of a people, it makes more sense to say that the Bible got it wrong. Randal Rauser, himself a Christian, raises equally pointed questions. Warrior, writing from the experience of Native peoples, reminds us that later generations have used this story to justify seizing land and killing, and that for the victims it reads like a completely different book. These challenges deserve a direct answer and should not be treated as malice.
The word “destroy”

The Hebrew word ḥērem is often translated “utterly destroy,” and its meaning is related to “set apart for God, not to be taken for use.” The stele of King Mesha of Moab (about 840 BC) also records that after capturing Nebo he killed about 7,000 people, “devoting” them to his god, which shows that this was a concept of war shared among the surrounding peoples of that time. Jeremiah 25:9 uses the same word of Judah, and yet some people from Judah in fact remained in the land. This supports the idea that the language was flexible, but it also reminds us that the seven thousand on Mesha’s stele really did die.
To be honest, we need to separate the facts, the debates and the inferences.
Joshua, Deuteronomy and 1 Samuel do contain language that includes women and children and says “leave no one”; other passages also record that large numbers of Canaanites survived.
Ancient Near Eastern war records often use the language of total victory. The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) declares “Israel is laid waste, his seed is not,” and Israel clearly did not perish.

K. Lawson Younger compared Assyrian, Hittite and Egyptian campaign accounts and argued that “the whole land” and “leave no one” in Joshua belong to the same kind of rhetoric. Many evangelical scholars follow this view, while other evangelical scholars consider it insufficient to explain the command itself.

Scholars are deeply divided over how far this conquest took place in history. Critical scholars such as Ronald Hendel think that Jericho and Ai were uninhabited in that period and that Israel most likely emerged gradually in the hill country. Conservative scholars such as Hess read the evidence differently. And even if it never happened in history, the question of “the text describes God this way” still remains.

The Old Testament’s laws on slavery have a protective side (Exodus 21:26-27; Deuteronomy 23:15-16) and a side that still jars us today (Exodus 21:20-21; Leviticus 25:44-46). Copan argues that this is a gradual process moving toward a higher ethic; critics consider it legislation for an evil institution all the same.

God has the authority to judge, the commands belonged to a particular time and place and cannot be repeated, and Christ is God’s clearest revelation of Himself. Taken together, these inferences can let believers carry on trusting while their questions remain open, but that does not mean the problem has been solved.
Who stands on which side of the line

The line in this war was not drawn entirely by bloodline. The Canaanite prostitute Rahab turned to the God of Israel, and her name entered the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Achan, an Israelite, stole what was devoted to destruction and fell under judgment himself (Joshua 7). Later Judah also went into exile, measured by the same ruler. God warned the Israelites against thinking themselves righteous:
Not for your righteousness or for the uprightness of your heart do you go in to possess their land; but for the wickedness of these nations
None of this lightens the weight of the texts. But it lets us see that the Old Testament itself does not portray God as a war god who cares for just one nation. He says:
I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live.
Where we must look in the end
Philip asked Jesus to show him the Father, and Jesus answered:
He who has seen me has seen the Father.

When the disciples wanted to call down fire from heaven as Elijah did, Jesus turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:54-55). When Peter drew a sword, He told him to put it away. And in the end, instead of swinging a sword at anyone else, He walked up to the cross Himself.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness.

The cross does not hand us an answer for every difficult verse. It answers a different and deeper question: is God indifferent to the evil of this world and to the blood of the innocent? His answer was to enter violence in person and bear the judgment. What we still do not understand, we entrust to this Judge who was once crucified.

Turn to 1 Samuel 15:3 and read it slowly, without rushing to explain it. Then turn to Luke 23 and read the account of Jesus being crucified. Lay both passages before God together, and tell Him what you really feel. People in the Psalms asked the same way: “How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1)
Reflect: Have I ever said things I did not believe myself, just to defend God? Or have I refused to get to know Jesus a little better because of a few verses?

Prayer: Lord, Judge of all the earth, these passages distress me, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Forgive my carelessness when I do not understand, and forgive the cruelty that people have done in Your name. Help me to know the Lord who died on the cross for His enemies, and teach me to act justly and love mercy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: a standard is not something you pick and choose from. Read the hard passages too, and read them in light of the whole Bible and ultimately in light of Christ.

Jesus is my example: today no one has the right to cite these passages to harm any person or any people. Whoever uses the Bible to justify violence, land seizure or domestic abuse has turned away from Christ.
Humility overcomes pride: let God be God, and let people be people. You can say plainly, “I don’t have an answer for this yet, but the Jesus I know makes me willing to keep trusting.”

blocks.h: This week: read Joshua 2 and 6, paying attention to Rahab. Write down one real question you have for God, and bring it to your small group or ask a pastor. If you have been wounded by war, violence or someone hurting you in God’s name, please find a pastor you trust and qualified professionals. Get yourself safe first, and then talk it through slowly.
Pass it on: Which part of the Old Testament do you find hardest to accept? There are places I struggle to read too, and I’d like to hear what you think.
Quiz

quiz.q: On the language of “leave no one,” what is the main argument of the “war rhetoric” school?
o: Ancient war records often used hyperbole, and the Bible itself records many survivors
All the Old Testament commands were forged by later writers
The Canaanites never existed
quiz.e: The main arguments of Copan and others are a comparison of literary genres and the Bible’s own records of survivors.

quiz.q: What is one serious challenge to the “war rhetoric” explanation?
o: Judges never mentions Canaanites
There were no wars in ancient times
Saul was rebuked precisely for leaving someone alive, so the wording of the command is hard to read entirely as hyperbole
quiz.e: 1 Samuel 15 is one of the hardest texts for this school to handle, which is one reason the debate is still unresolved.

quiz.q: What do these passages mean for Christians today?
o: They can be applied in the same way to today’s enemies
No one has the right to cite them to defend violence; God’s heart must be seen through Christ
They should be deleted from the Bible
quiz.e: Whichever explanation they take, evangelicals do not treat these commands as a model for today. Jesus is God’s clearest revelation of Himself.

units.title: The Bible and Science
units.sub: The Bible says the sun rises and sets, and so does the TV weather presenter. Neither one is wrong.

share.v: All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.

blocks.h: In 1615 Galileo, in a long letter, cited a saying he said he had heard from a high-ranking churchman: the Holy Spirit’s purpose is to teach us how to go to heaven, not how the heavens go. Later scholars generally take that churchman to be Cardinal Baronius, though no document directly proves it.

More than four hundred years later, that saying still stands between two kinds of people: those who treat the Bible as an astronomy textbook, and those who are sure science has made the Bible obsolete. Before turning to the first page of the Bible, perhaps we should first ask: what question is this book trying to answer?
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.
Two books, one Author

In The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon urged people not to think they had already put enough work into either the book of God’s word or the book of God’s works. Both the Bible and nature deserve study, but each with the right method, and the two must not be confused with each other.

As early as the beginning of the fifth century, Augustine warned that it is shameful and dangerous when a Christian talks nonsense about sun, moon and stars and claims that this is what the Bible means, so that those who know better laugh at him, because people will then stop believing even the message of the resurrection.
God stoops to our language

Calvin was very direct when he commented on the “two great lights” in Genesis 1:16. Astronomers know that Saturn is larger than the moon; it just looks small because it is far away. Moses wrote for ordinary people, so he used the way of speaking that everyone could understand. In the Institutes he also says that God speaks to us the way a nurse speaks baby talk to a child. This is called “accommodation”: God speaks in language the people of that time could understand, which does not mean He is teaching erroneous knowledge.

When the weather presenter says, “Sunrise tomorrow is at 6:12,” no astronomer phones in to correct her. She is describing what is seen from the ground. And when you tell a five-year-old, “The baby came from Mommy’s tummy,” you are not lying. It is a true thing he can understand right now.
The heavens as the ancients saw them

What exactly is the “expanse” of Genesis 1:6-8 (Hebrew rāqîaʿ, rendered “firmament” in older English translations)? Paul Seely argues that people then imagined a solid dome with water above it. Vern Poythress replies that the text describes what is seen and does not propose a physical theory. John Walton holds that Genesis 1 is ancient cosmology, concerned with function and order: God establishing the cosmos as His temple, rather than saying where matter came from.

items.h: Reads Genesis by the literal six 24-hour days, and holds that the Bible’s chronology takes priority over the dates reckoned by mainstream geology and cosmology.
The “days” can refer to long periods, and the order of creation corresponds roughly to natural history.

The seven days are a deliberately arranged literary structure: the first three days form the realms and the last three fill them with inhabitants. The point is theological and not a chronological sequence.

The text is about God giving the cosmos its functions and taking up residence in it. It does not directly answer the question of the origin of matter, so it is not on the same level as scientific questions about age.

blocks.h: Each of these is held by serious evangelical believers, each has its strengths, and each has its difficulties. These differences do not touch the core of the faith: God is the Creator.
Joshua’s sun and Galileo

Joshua 10:12-13 says the sun “stood still.” In 1539 a student recorded Luther’s reaction at the dinner table when the conversation turned to Copernicus: he believed the Bible, because it was the sun that Joshua commanded to stand still, not the earth. The oft-quoted line attributed to Calvin, “Who will dare to place the authority of Copernicus above that of the Holy Spirit?”, has no documentary support. The historian Edward Rosen traced it to a reconstruction from memory by F. W. Farrar in the nineteenth century, which was then spread by A. D. White. Calvin did preach one sermon criticizing the claim that “the sun does not move,” but he did not name Copernicus, and his exact view remains unclear to this day.

Readers do not agree on this passage either. Some take it as a real miracle recorded from an observer’s point of view. Others note that the words are cited from the Book of Jashar and have a poetic character. Galileo himself even proposed an ingenious reading, but it was only a debating point.

In 1615 Cardinal Robert Bellarmine wrote that if someone really did prove the sun-centered view, then we would have to say that we had not understood those passages, and not that Scripture was wrong; he simply did not believe such a proof existed. Believers today would do well to remember this sentence.
Some of this is historical fact, and some is interpretation. Let’s look at them separately.

In 1616 the theological consultants of the Roman Curia judged the sun-centered view to be a heretical proposition. In 1633 Galileo was found “vehemently suspect of heresy” and forced to recant, and after the verdict he was kept under house arrest for a long time. But he was not tortured and hardly spent time in prison; the familiar story of “dungeons and torture” belongs to later legend.

Calvin explicitly held that Moses used popular speech. In commenting on Genesis 1:16 he acknowledged that the astronomers’ knowledge is correct, and explained that Moses used the language of ordinary people.

Most ancient Near Eastern people imagined the sky as some kind of solid structure, a point much discussed. But whether the Genesis “expanse” teaches this view of the cosmos is still debated among evangelicals.

Article XII of the evangelical Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy does not accept limiting the Bible’s reliability to matters of faith and salvation while leaving out its assertions in history and science, and Article XIII says that observational descriptions of natural phenomena do not affect inerrancy. This tension has to be faced honestly: not all evangelicals agree that “the Bible only teaches how to go to heaven.”

Claims such as “the Bible predicted modern science long ago” mostly fail under close examination. Job 26:7 says God “hangs the earth on nothing,” yet the same Bible also speaks of “the pillars of the earth” (1 Samuel 2:8) and “the foundations of the earth” (Job 38:4-6). These are all poetry, and if you treat one as science, you have to treat the others as science too.

Nature and the Bible come from the same God, so true facts and correct interpretation will in the end not contradict each other. This is a conviction, not an experimental result; science can neither prove nor disprove God.
The “circle of the earth” in Isaiah 40:22

Isaiah 40:22 speaks of God sitting above “the circle of the earth” (the Chinese Union Version renders this as “the great circle of the globe”), and people often say the Bible knew long ago that the earth is round. Notice the second half of the same verse: He “stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in.” This is poetry, and the Hebrew word means a circle or an arc, not a technical term for a sphere. The Chinese word for “globe” is the translators’ choice. We do not need to win Isaiah an astronomy prize he never meant to compete for. His point is that God is immensely great and people are very small, so do not be afraid.
The ultimate stooping
God has always spoken in a way people can understand, and in His deepest act of all, He Himself became the Word.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

Calvin said God speaks like a nurse babbling to a child. At Bethlehem the Lord who holds all things together truly became an infant who could not speak, and in the end, as Philippians 2:8 says, “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” Three days later He rose from the dead. Science can describe the distances of the stars, but it cannot tell you that the Lord who made the stars was willing to be nailed to a cross for you. This is what the Bible wants to tell us.
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.
Tonight, step outside and look up at the moon or at any bright star. Think of what Calvin said: Saturn is larger than the moon and only looks small because it is far away. Then read Psalm 8:3-4.
Meditate: Am I afraid that science will shake my faith, and so I do not dare to ask? Or do I lean on science news to prop up my confidence, forgetting that I believe in a living Lord?

Pray: Lord who created heaven and earth, thank You for stooping to our weak understanding, even becoming flesh and dying on the cross. Give us minds that fear You, that dare to explore and also dare to admit they do not know. Let us worship You through both of Your books. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: A standard has to be read according to its genre. Read poetry as poetry and history as history, and do not force it to answer questions it is not answering.

Humility overcomes pride: When we differ on the date of creation, there is no need to sort people into categories and pronounce them guilty. Unity in the core, generosity at the edges, and people matter more than winning the argument.
Change your mindset: Move science out of the enemy’s seat. If your child wants to study science or engineering, pray for him, and worship with him the Lord who made all things.

blocks.h: This week: Find one “the Bible said it long ago” claim about a scientific discovery that you have heard. Open the passage and read the five verses before and after it. Ask yourself: what is the genre of this passage? What was the author trying to say to the people of his time?
Pass it on: Do you think science and faith must be at war? How did you form that impression?
Quiz

quiz.q: What does “accommodation” mean?
o: Everything recorded in the Bible is erroneous knowledge
God speaks in a way that people of that time could understand
Christians should revise the Bible to suit the times
quiz.e: Calvin pointed out that Moses wrote in popular language so that everyone could understand. That does not mean the Bible teaches error.

quiz.q: Which statement about Galileo is closer to the historical facts?
o: He was found “vehemently suspect of heresy” and kept under house arrest for a long time, but he was not tortured
He was held in a dungeon and tortured
He was never tried by the Church
quiz.e: The trial and sentence of 1633 are real; the dungeon and torture are later legend.

quiz.q: Why is it unwise to say that “Job 26:7 predicted modern astronomy”?
o: Because Job is not part of the Bible
Because the earth is not suspended in space
Because it is poetry, and the same Bible also uses the poetic language of “foundations” and “pillars”
quiz.e: If you treat one passage as science, you have to treat the other as science too. Reading by genre is being faithful to the Bible.

units.title: The Book That Changes Lives
units.sub: A child’s singing, a sinking ship, a letter from a pastor. What they met was the same Book.

share.v: For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword

blocks.h: In AD 386, in a garden in Milan, a successful professor of rhetoric collapsed in tears under a fig tree. From next door came the sound of a child singing over and over: “Take up and read, take up and read.” He opened Paul’s letters and read a passage.
not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.

His name was Augustine. More than thirteen hundred years later, a man in London listened as someone read aloud Luther’s preface to that same letter to the Romans, and he felt his heart grow strangely warm. How can this book cross so many centuries and keep touching people?
Six people, one thread

items: Augustine (386): In Book VIII of his Confessions he records the scene in the garden. His friend Alypius read on and came to “Now accept one who is weak in faith,” and applied the sentence to himself.

Luther: Looking back in 1545, he said that he had hated the very words “God’s righteousness” in Romans 1:17, until he understood “the righteous shall live by faith,” and felt as if he had been born again and had gone through open gates into paradise.

Wesley (1738): On the morning of 24 May he read 2 Peter 1:4, and in the evening he went, rather unwillingly, to a meeting on Aldersgate Street. At about a quarter to nine, his heart felt strangely warmed, and he felt that he did trust in Christ, Christ alone.
John Newton (1748): A sailor who had been involved in the slave trade off West Africa, he met a storm in the Atlantic, read the New Testament aboard ship, and took hold of Luke 11:13.

Rosaria Butterfield (1999): A tenured professor of English and women’s studies at Syracuse University. A pastor wrote her a letter with questions, and she became friends with the pastor and his wife for two years and read the Bible through several times.
Nabeel Qureshi: Raised in a devout Ahmadiyya Muslim family, in 2001 he saw his classmate David Wood reading the Bible alone, and began debating him, which went on for several years.

blocks.h: These are all records the people themselves left, and you can look up the original books.

A seed left in a drawer for ten years is still a seed. It is not a magic pill; it needs soil, water and time. In these stories the Book never works alone: Augustine had his mother and Ambrose, Butterfield had the Smiths’ dinner table, and Qureshi had his friend Wood.
The stories are not that tidy

Newton’s story is often told as if, the moment the storm hit, the slave ship turned around. In fact after his conversion he still served as first mate and then captain on slave ships, did not leave the sea until a stroke in 1754, and continued to invest afterward. Only in 1788 did he publish Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade, calling himself an active instrument in that business, a lifelong shame. By then it had been 34 years since he left the sea. Wesley, too, kept struggling after Aldersgate; as late as 4 January 1739 he wrote that he was not a Christian. And in his old age Luther wrote some viciously anti-Jewish texts.

C. S. Lewis’s road was also long. He described how in 1929 he knelt and admitted that God was God, “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England” (his biographer Alister McGrath thinks it was 1930). In September 1931 he talked late into the night at Oxford with Tolkien and Dyson, and only a few days later accepted that Jesus is the Son of God. He later wrote in a letter that the story of Christ is a myth that really happened.
That “four times”

The Center for Bible Engagement in the United States has surveyed more than 150,000 people over nearly two decades. Its report says that people who engage with the Bible four or more days a week have 62% lower odds of being drunk habitually and are about 59% less likely to view pornography (the report does not state its statistical definitions), and they also share their faith and give more often. This is an encouraging correlation, but note its limits: the data are mostly self-reported questionnaires; the organization itself promotes Bible reading and so has a stake; the article mentions peer review but names no journal; and people who are already serious may both read the Bible more and err less. It cannot prove that “four times and you will be changed.”
Testimonies are moving, but it matters even more to be clear about which parts can be stated with certainty.
Augustine, Luther, Wesley, Newton, Lewis, Butterfield and Qureshi each left a firsthand account saying that the Bible played a key role in their change.

Most of these accounts were written many years afterward and shaped by their authors. Some scholars think Augustine’s garden scene was literarily shaped, though that is no reason to deny the event; the timing of Luther’s breakthrough is also disputed, and James Kittelson thinks it was around 1518 to 1521 and came about gradually.
Engaging with the Bible four or more days a week is associated with fewer self-reported problem behaviors. This is a report from an organization’s own research, and correlation is not causation.

The Bible does not automatically make people better. Some people read it and defended slavery, and some scholars who studied it seriously left the faith; Bart Ehrman, for example, says the problem of suffering was the key to his loss of faith.

Christians believe that the root of these changes is God at work through His word and the Holy Spirit. Testimonies cannot prove this, and other religions also have life-changing stories, but they make “this book is worth reading for yourself” a reasonable invitation.
At the center of the Book is a Person
Jesus said something very weighty to people who knew the Scriptures well:
“You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.
So what changes people is not paper and ink. On the evening of the resurrection, two heartbroken disciples met a stranger on the road, who opened the Scriptures to them.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”

Seventeen hundred years later Wesley’s heart was also “strangely warmed.” The One who opened the Scriptures to them is the Jesus who was crucified and rose again. He is alive today, which is why this book is more than a record. What Romans 1:17 showed Luther was also the righteousness God gives freely at the cross of Christ.
I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me

This also explains why everyone in these stories paid a price and yet the change went on. Butterfield says she counted the cost and did not like the number on the other side of the equals sign. Qureshi lost most of his Muslim friends and died of stomach cancer at 34. The Bible never promised smooth sailing. What it promises is a Lord who is with you.

Open to John chapter 1 and read slowly through the first 14 verses. Before you read, pray this simple prayer: “If You are real, please let me know You.” When you finish, circle one line that stays with you, and sit quietly for two minutes.
Meditate: Do I read the Bible to finish a schedule, or to meet a living Lord? Which verse has ever taken hold of me?

Pray: Lord Jesus, Your word is a lamp to my feet. Thank You that You spoke to sinners like Augustine, Luther and Newton, and that You speak to me today. Holy Spirit, shine Your light on me, so that I do not only read but am willing to obey, and let my heart burn again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: Set a goal so small that you cannot fail. One passage of John each day, using the 321 Interactive Bible, finishes in twenty-one days.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: Before reading, ask the Holy Spirit to open the text; after reading, ask one question: what does He want me to change today? Changing your mindset is what changes your life and how you live.
People matter more than tasks: The Smiths gave two years at their dinner table, and Wood gave years of friendship. Accompanying one person in reading the Bible does more than winning an argument.

blocks.h: This week: Starting today, read John chapter 1, and invite a family member or friend to read it with you. About once a week, trade the one line each of you circled.
Pass it on: Have you ever read a bit of the Bible? Would you like to read John chapter 1 together, and afterward tell me what you honestly think, good or bad?
Quiz

quiz.q: What was being read aloud when Wesley was at Aldersgate in 1738?
o: Luther’s preface to Romans
Augustine’s Confessions
Newton’s hymns
quiz.e: The Bible’s letter to the Romans reached Wesley through Luther, a thread that spans several centuries.

quiz.q: What happened to John Newton after his conversion?
o: He left the slave trade that very day
He never regretted anything
He served for years as a slave-ship captain, and spoke out publicly against the slave trade only in 1788
quiz.e: Change is often a long process. His testimony carries more weight because it is honest, and it reminds us to recognize the blind spots of conscience.

quiz.q: How should we best understand the research on reading the Bible “four or more times a week”?
o: It proves that four times a week guarantees change
It shows a correlation, mostly self-reported, and cannot prove causation
It proves that people who do not read the Bible must be worse
quiz.e: Data like this is worth consulting, but correlation is not causation, and it should not be used to condemn people.

questions.q: The Bible was copied so many times. Isn’t it full of errors?
Why does the God of the Old Testament seem so cruel?
